To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
three-dimensional, active-site profiling can be used to identify members of protein functional families with high confidence.

we developed a method to identify active site profiles that can be used for functional annotation of protein sequences, and this method was applied to a large set of protein kinases and shown to correctly classify the subfamily of the kinase.

structure-based active-site profiling provides a powerful method to classify and identify members of protein functional families, and this method has been used successfully to classify and identify the subtypes of protein kinases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of protein functional families based on the structural similarity of their active sites.
the use of structural information to identify and characterize functional families, and to provide a basis for functional classification of proteins that lack structural information.
the development and application of a structure-based approach for functional site analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the three-dimensional active-site profiles developed for this work provide a powerful tool for genome analysis, functional family subclassification, and drug design.
the method of active-site profiling described here provides a means to characterize the structural environment surrounding a functional site.
three-dimensional active site profiles provide a unique and powerful method for genome annotation, and are a valuable addition to other methods for protein family identification.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the method described here can be used for genome analysis and for detailed subclassification of protein function.
we have developed a structure-based method of active-site profiling for use in genome analysis and functional classification.

the three-dimensional, or structural, active-site profiles developed in this work provide a powerful tool for the identification and subclassification of protein families, and for the identification and annotation of functional families in genome sequences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structure of the active site of a protein is a more reliable predictor of its function than the global structure of the protein or its sequence.
the three-dimensional active site profiles are a powerful tool for the classification of functional protein family members, including those with unknown structure.
the active-site profile method is a powerful tool for functional classification of structurally unclassified proteins.
